title: Ocelot Medical — On‑Prem & VPC Security Architecture Review
topics: firewalling: security groups vs NACLs vs perimeter
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Ocelot Medical through a deep technical review of Private/VPC and on-prem deployment security. Main concerns: strict egress controls (no direct internet egress), key management and HSM requirements for patient data, audit log forwarding and retention to their SIEM, and RBAC/SSO provisioning. Discussed implementation patterns (private endpoints, NAT/proxy egress, bastionless admin flows), KMS key policies, offline HSM options, and required documents for SOC2 review. Next steps: exchange IP ranges & CIDRs, delivery of KMS onboarding checklist and SOC2 artifact packet, schedule hands-on lab to validate egress rules, follow-up architecture diagram update.
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Jamie Chen from Redwood Inference, I'll kick things off. Uh, we also have Ravi on the call who will do the technical deep dive. How's everything, Elena?
[00:12] Dr. Elena: Good thanks. We wanted to focus this session on the on-prem/VPC install details — network isolation, what you need from us for ingress/egress, and KMS. We're handling PHI so we need to be careful.
[00:24] Jamie: Absolutely. High level we'll cover: private endpoints, egress controls (we know you prefer no direct internet egress), firewalling patterns, and KMS/HSM integration — plus logs to your SIEM.
[00:33] Marcus: Quick qualifier: timeline is Q1 pilot, security signoff is gating. Also our infra team wants minimum attack surface; we don't want open ports or unnecessary NATs.
[00:44] Ravi: Good notes. I'll start with VPC layout options. Typical Redwood private deployment can either live in your VPC or in a customer-managed VPC peered to a Redwood-managed control plane. For on-prem we ship an appliance-like bundle; both use the same principles: isolate inference nodes in private subnets, control ingress via private endpoints, and manage egress through a constrained proxy or NAT with allowlists.
[01:08] Sophie: When you say "private endpoints" do you mean AWS PrivateLink or something equivalent? We avoid traversal over public internet for any control plane talk.
[01:16] Ravi: Yes, AWS PrivateLink or GCP VPC peering equivalents. In on-prem cases we use mutual TLS over an outbound-only connection to the Redwood control plane — that might be misheard in notes as "mTLS outbound tunnel" — but essentially there is no inbound hole from the internet.
[01:30] Jamie: Important to call out: we support an outbound-only model where the data plane calls home over an egress proxy controlled by you, and our control plane can't initiate inbound connections.
[01:40] Dr. Elena: Our security policy says zero direct egress except to pre-approved endpoints and through an enterprise proxy. Can Redwood work with that?
[01:47] Jamie: Yes. The typical approach is: 1) configure your egress firewall to only allow HTTPS to a specific set of Redwood IP ranges and FQDNs, 2) use your corporate proxy with authenticated egress, or 3) for fully air-gapped, use a scheduled sync/transfer via secure media. We can provide IP ranges and TLS fingerprint data.
[02:05] Marcus: Are the IP ranges stable? We need to add them to our allowlist and our change window is tight.
[02:11] Ravi: We'll provide a CIDR block and a signed IP list; we also support announcing via a prefix that you can route via your transit gateway. For low-change requirements we can set up a dedicated peering or PrivateLink which avoids frequent updates.
[02:25] Sophie: On key management: we need an HSM-backed KMS with customer key rotation policy. Keys must never be exported. How is encryption in rest/in transit handled?
[02:37] Ravi: All model artifacts and KV cache are encrypted at rest with envelope encryption. We integrate with customer KMS — AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or customer HSM via an on-prem connector. Keys are used inside the runtime but we can restrict operations: encrypt/decrypt by policy bound to instance role. We also support HSM appliances where the private key material is never on disk — we call that the HSM-protected keyflow.
[02:59] Jamie: Note that for SOC2/ISO you should expect key rotation logs and key use audit trails; we'll include KMS audit events in the log stream we forward to your SIEM.
[03:09] Dr. Elena: That log forwarding — is it agent-based or do you ship logs to S3 and we pull?
[03:15] Ravi: Multiple options. For VPC: we push structured logs to your log collector via a secure forwarding pipeline (TLS + mutual auth). Alternatively we can write to your S3/GCS bucket using VPC endpoint and you ingest. For on-prem, we run a local log agent that forwards to your splunk/qradar endpoint. Some customers prefer fluentd/collector sidecar.
[03:32] Aamir: We need 7-year retention for audit records per internal policy — is that supported?
[03:39] Jamie: We can store logs for long-term retention as an add-on; out-of-the-box retention windows are shorter but enterprise retention is available. We'll provide export capability so you can keep raw logs in your archive.
[03:50] Marcus: Firewalling: recommended layers? We use security groups for instance-level rules but want an additional perimeter.
[03:58] Ravi: Defense in depth: security groups + NACLs + transit gateway route controls + perimeter NGFW if you have one. Within the cluster we recommend Kubernetes NetworkPolicies (if running on k8s) or host-level firewall (iptables/eBPF) to restrict pod-to-pod. For model serving we segment by workload — inference pool in one subnet, admin interfaces in another locked to a jump host.
[04:20] Sophie: Admin access — do you require bastion hosts? We prefer ephemeral admin sessions via SSO and audit.
[04:27] Ravi: We integrate with SAML/OIDC so you can do SSO into the Redwood Console. For on-prem host-level access we support proxy jump through your bastion or a session manager; we can also integrate with privileged access tools to avoid open bastions. All admin actions are logged with user identity.
[04:43] Dr. Elena: Are there any ports we need to open inbound?
[04:48] Jamie: For the outbound-only model, no inbound ports need to be open to the inference nodes. Only your management plane for on-prem might need a port for admin if you want direct SSH, but we strongly advise session-managed admin via your PAM.
[04:59] Marcus: Network egress for model downloads — how does that work? We want the model artifacts to come from a secure repo, not public mirrors.
[05:06] Ravi: You can host model artifacts in a private artifact repo (S3 bucket or on-prem NFS). The deployment process will fetch artifacts over your internal network or via PrivateLink. We can seed nodes via your bootstrap mechanism so no public access is required.
[05:21] Jamie: Also discussed: prefix/KV cache — sorry that's "KV cache" — we can pin caches to local disk and encrypt them; they can also be stored on an internal filesystem behind the same egress controls.
[05:33] Sophie: How about intrusion detection and anomaly detection — do you expose runtime telemetry?
[05:38] Ravi: We push metrics and tracing — we can feed into your Prometheus/SIEM. For IDS, we recommend exporting netflow and audit logs to your SOC, and we can enable additional runtime audit hooks for suspicious API patterns. There's a small perf cost for extreme-level audit sampling, we'll quantify for you.
[05:58] Dr. Elena: Ok let's talk SSO & RBAC. We need SCIM provisioning and fine-grained RBAC so devs only have inference-only roles, security staff have audit-only.
[06:08] Jamie: We support SAML/OIDC and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with resource scoping (by project/model/environment). You can map SAML groups to Redwood roles. We'll share the RBAC matrix template.
[06:20] Marcus: For evidence, what SOC2 artifacts can you provide?
[06:25] Jamie: We can provide SOC2 Type II report, ISO docs on request, encryption architecture diagrams, KMS integration checklist, and a snapshot of controls for deployment. For any redactions we have a process. We'll deliver those as part of the compliance package.
[06:38] Sophie: We need to validate the KMS integration — can we run a hands-on lab where we rotate keys and observe behavior?
[06:44] Ravi: Yes, we recommend a lab: 1) provision a test key in your KMS, 2) deploy a small inference pool in a test VPC with your egress proxy, 3) rotate the key and confirm no downtime and audit events. We can staff the lab with an SE.
[06:59] Jamie: Next, ingress for customer traffic — do you plan to route inference requests through your own API gateway or query Redwood endpoints directly?
[07:08] Marcus: We prefer routing through our API gateway to apply extra auth and rate limits. We want the model runtime not exposed publicly.
[07:14] Ravi: That's fine. Many customers front the inference endpoints behind their API gateway inside the VPC, with an internal-only ALB or NLB and strict TLS mTLS to clients.
[07:26] Dr. Elena: Anything we should be aware of with regard to data residency and backup snapshots? Snapshots are sensitive.
[07:34] Ravi: Snapshots are encrypted and can be disabled. If you require that snapshots never leave your site, we can use local-only persistence. For the hosted control plane variant we do store a minimal metadata set — you can opt for a fully private control plane to avoid that.
[07:49] Sophie: Can you describe the exact log fields you forward for KMS events? We need SSH-like traceability: who did what, when, source IP and principal.
[07:58] Ravi: KMS events include key-id, operation (encrypt/decrypt/GenerateDataKey), principal ARN, timestamp, and a request ID. We also annotate with instance-id and deployment-id for traceability. We'll provide a sample log schema.
[08:11] Aamir: For on-prem HSM, what's the recommended vendor? We have Thales and Intel—compatibility?
[08:18] Ravi: We support common PKCS#11 HSMs (Thales, Luna) and cloud HSMs. For appliances we use an HSM connector that talks PKCS#11; your security team can review key policies. If you need FIPS or specific certifications, we can validate.
[08:33] Dr. Elena: Are there any known limitations if we require full air gap?
[08:39] Jamie: Full air gap increases operational overhead. Model updates become manual or via signed packages; telemetry is limited. We support scheduled export/import workflows and an on-prem-only control plane, but you sacrifice some automation like live patching or auto-scaling without additional orchestration. We'll document the tradeoffs in the onboarding guide.
[08:58] Marcus: A few nitty-gritty Qs: do you require outbound DNS? We restrict DNS egress tightly.
[09:05] Ravi: DNS can be solved locally — we only need to resolve Redwood FQDNs for outbound TLS. If you have internal resolver that forwards for approved domains, that's fine. We also support pinning by IP and certificate thumbprint to avoid DNS entirely.
[09:18] Sophie: How are secrets injected into the runtime for private KMS?
[09:23] Ravi: We support secrets via your secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) with short-lived ephemeral credentials. There is an option to use a sealed-secret approach for Kubernetes with automatic unsealing via your KMS.
[09:36] Dr. Elena: Can we get a network diagram and a runbook for incident response? We need IP addresses to monitor.
[09:42] Jamie: Yes — we'll send an architecture diagram template and an incident runbook. The runbook will include steps for isolating nodes, rotating keys, and toggling fallback to a stable model variant if you need to degrade gracefully.
[09:56] Marcus: On fallback: if you lose connectivity to your KMS, can the runtime continue serving?
[10:02] Ravi: For security we avoid keeping plaintext keys; you can allow a short cached data key for brief outages, subject to policy you set. The better pattern is degrade to a read-only mode or fail closed. We'll work with you to set your desired behavior.
[10:15] Sophie: About audit trails — who has access to raw audit logs inside Redwood? We need guarantees that only our account principals see them.
[10:22] Ravi: In private deployments the logs live in your systems or S3 — your permissions control access. For hosted variants we keep per-customer isolated logs accessible only to authorized support with an approval workflow and audit trail.
[10:36] Jamie: Let's cover the SOC2 artifact timeline: we can provide a redacted SOC2 Type II immediately, full on request subject to NDA. Also a deployment checklist and KMS onboarding doc.
[10:47] Dr. Elena: Good. Sophie — any more deep tech asks?
[10:51] Sophie: One last: can we require mutual TLS between our API gateway and the inference pool?
[10:56] Ravi: Yes, we support mTLS. We can accept client certs signed by your CA and verify on the load balancer.
[11:04] Aamir: For the hands-on lab, what logs should we capture?
[11:09] Ravi: Capture KMS audit events, netflow, application access logs, and the runtime's structured request logs. We'll provide a lab capture checklist.
[11:19] Jamie: Ok let's recap and assign next steps.
[11:22] Dr. Elena: Thanks, this was helpful.
[11:26] [End of recording — note: transcript auto-truncated at this point for brevity, full call ~72 minutes with Q&A, screen-share of network diagrams and a short demo of KMS rotation behavior. Some words mis-transcribed (e.g., "mT L S" for mTLS, "KV cash" for KV cache).]
